langLift.title: LangLift – Full-Stack Language Learning Platform
langLift.summary: Designed and built a full-stack language-learning platform with spaced-repetition study sets, instant "quick study" sessions, and AI-assisted moderation/verification for user-generated content. Built with Python/FastAPI, React/TypeScript, MongoDB, and Google Cloud Platform.
langLift.architectureBody1: Architected the backend for a language-learning web app using Python (FastAPI), MongoDB Atlas, and Google Cloud Run, with React/TypeScript on the frontend and Cloudflare for CDN and domain routing.
langLift.architectureBody2: Designed the core data model around cards, decks, and study sets, treating cards as reusable entities that can be shared across decks and personalized via per-user study state.
langLift.architectureBody3: Implemented a service-oriented architecture with separate flows for long-term study, quick preview sessions, content moderation, and card verification, making it easy to scale features independently.
langLift.architectureBody4: Defined and implemented MongoDB schemas and indexes for high-volume study traffic, including TTL-based session collections and due-date-indexed study cards to support efficient scheduling queries.
langLift.studySystemBody1: Designed and documented a durable Study-Set Session flow driven by the SM-2 spaced-repetition algorithm, with per-user fields like ease, interval, due, reps, and status persisted per prompt variant.
langLift.studySystemBody2: Implemented per-day review and new-card caps at the study-set level, along with atomic counters that reset and update automatically based on date boundaries.
langLift.studySystemBody3: Built a session system that maintains a 30-card queue with a 5-card front-end buffer, dynamically refilling from due reviews and new cards while respecting the user's daily limits.
langLift.studySystemBody4: Designed a robust answer pipeline where each answer atomically pops the next study card, runs the SM-2 update, updates daily stats, refills the queue when it falls below a threshold, and returns the next hydrated card and updated stats.
langLift.quickStudyBody1: Designed a separate Quick Study session flow for instant, low-friction deck review that intentionally avoids touching the user's long-term SM-2 data.
langLift.quickStudyBody2: Implemented a lightweight quick_study_session collection with TTL (~2 hours), tracking user_id, deck_id, seen_ids, and a small queue of card variants.
langLift.quickStudyBody3: Built a queue refill algorithm that scans deck cards in deck order, applies a prompt-offset rule to space front/back variants, skips cards already seen, and maintains up to 30 pending items while the client always holds 5 in memory.
langLift.moderationBody1: Designed an automated moderation pipeline for user-generated cards and decks that combines first-pass scoring with Google Perspective API for toxicity/profanity, followed by secondary LLM-based review (Claude 3, GPT-4o) for nuanced decisions.
langLift.moderationBody2: Defined a Moderation Document schema to track each flagged item with fields for content type, submitter, initial toxicity scores, LLM verdict and reasoning, status, and resolution notes.
langLift.moderationBody3: Integrated moderation status directly into card/deck metadata so the UI can hide or downgrade risky content, with a planned admin dashboard for reviewing unresolved moderation docs.
langLift.verificationBody1: Designed a card verification pipeline to improve accuracy and trust in definitions, supporting both manual requests from high-tier premium users and automatic triggers when cards become popular.
langLift.verificationBody2: Created a per-language verification metadata block on each card (status, last_verified_at, method, verifier) so users can see which translations have been AI- or human-verified.
langLift.verificationBody3: Implemented language-level AI validation settings allowing creators to decide which languages use AI auto-verification vs manual control, with AI models checking grammar, factual accuracy, and cross-language alignment.
langLift.resilienceBody1: Designed APIs and flows to be resilient to real-world usage: double taps, multi-tab sessions, flaky networks, and partial offline usage.
langLift.resilienceBody2: Added guardrails for multi-tab and offline usage (idempotent answer endpoints, optional active_tab_token, offline answer queues on the client), preventing double-counting and race conditions.
langLift.resilienceBody3: Planned an offline premium mode that preloads ~1,000 upcoming cards, runs SM-2 locally, logs answers client-side, and replays them on the server for reconciliation.
langLift.conclusion: This project demonstrates expertise in full-stack architecture, algorithm design (SM-2 spaced repetition), AI/ML integration, and building production-ready systems that handle real-world edge cases. Separated "long-term learning" (SM-2 Study Sets) from "quick preview/cram" (Quick Study) to match real learner workflows while avoiding noise in spaced-repetition statistics.

kanjiTrainer.title: Kanji Trainer for Raspberry Pi
kanjiTrainer.intro: Developed a spaced repetition application using the SM2 algorithm (SuperMemo) to help users learn Japanese kanji and words efficiently. This project was designed specifically to run on Raspberry Pi, making it an accessible learning tool for Japanese language students.
kanjiTrainer.technicalBody: The application was configured and optimized to run on Raspberry Pi, leveraging Linux and Python 3.11. I utilized SDL2 and SDL2-TTF for graphical rendering, which provided smooth performance on the Raspberry Pi hardware. The application integrated an SQLite database containing the top 3000 kanji with stroke order data, allowing users to practice writing kanji correctly.
kanjiTrainer.developmentBody1: To streamline the setup process, I automated installation procedures using Poetry for dependency management. This ensured smooth installation of all required libraries and made it easy for users to get started with the application.
kanjiTrainer.developmentBody2: The spaced repetition system implemented the SM2 algorithm, which adapts learning intervals based on user performance. I implemented daily progress tracking, allowing users to see their improvement over time and maintain consistent study habits.
kanjiTrainer.performanceBody: During initial development, I encountered performance issues that affected the user experience. To address these, I reduced the polling rate and implemented a line smoothing algorithm to streamline the writing process. These optimizations resulted in a significantly faster and more responsive user experience, making the application much more enjoyable to use.
kanjiTrainer.conclusion: This project was a great learning experience in optimizing applications for resource-constrained hardware while maintaining a smooth user experience. It also deepened my understanding of spaced repetition algorithms and their practical applications in language learning.

gameDevelopment.title: Game Development
gameDevelopment.intro1BeforeLink: During my time in college, I decided to join the Game Development club. In the club we had a couple of workshops where we learned about different types of games as well as how to make them in unity. This game,
gameDevelopment.intro1AfterLink: , was the last workshop that we did which was about puzzle games.
gameDevelopment.intro2: So, my group decided to make a Christmas themed puzzle game since it was December. First let me tell you about the game a little bit and then I will talk about the prcoess that we used to develop the game.
gameDevelopment.intro3: The game is about a person with a multi-tool that has four main uses: blacklight, wrench, fishing rod, and a flute. Using the tool, you have to solve the puzzle in each room by finding the wishlist for that person's room. There are four rooms in total and each room focuses on two main uses of the flute. For the first room, which is the player's bedroom, you have to use the blacklight and the flute to get your cat, Tiny, out of the way. Then you enter the main house where you are able to continue your quest to find all of the wish lists.
gameDevelopment.body1: For this project, my main role was the level designer. So for the beginning of the project, I ended up leading the discussion about what type of game everyone wanted to make. At first, we were all giving a large range of ideas, but I had to take all of those ideas and put them together to make a game that we could feasibly finish within the 6 week time frame that we had been given.
gameDevelopment.body2: After I collected everyone's ideas and came up with a solid idea of what we wanted to do, I got to work with creating the blacklight, which presented a couple of challenges because of the way that unity handles light. The main issue was that light in unity is that it does actually tell other objects that it is interacting with it, so I had to put together a solution using HLSL to get the effect that I wanted. Then I had to design all of the rooms including a hedge maze and a tiled train puzzle where the player has to rotate tracks and get the right solution. Finally, after putting everything together, you can find the game that my team produced at this link:
gameDevelopment.conclusion: Overall, I had a lot of fun learning to code using HLSL and creating fun but difficult puzzles.

discordBots.title: Discord Bots
discordBots.intro1: In this project, I wanted to connect Discord and Twitter, by combing the two APIs and seamlessly connecting them together. So I set off to learn how to code using the discord API. My first project was very simple and it was the implementation of a queue. Using discord commands, you could easily join and leave the queue and I used it to keep track of who was playing AmongUs at the time.
discordBots.intro2: Since that went well, I continued my journey to creating a functioning Discord bot that would send the tweets of a user defined account to the corresponding user defined text channel.
discordBots.intro3: Overall, this project ended up being a good learning experience for me because I was able to see different ways of utilizing API as well as how I could use the API without straining it too much.

iotSimulator.title: IoT Sensor Simulator with Azure IoT Hub
iotSimulator.intro: Collaborated with a cross-functional team to design a robust IoT sensor simulation system for real-time monitoring. This project involved creating a comprehensive system that could simulate various sensor types and integrate seamlessly with Azure IoT Hub for cloud-based data management and visualization.
iotSimulator.devBody: I developed Python scripts to generate and send simulated sensor data (e.g., temperature, humidity) in JSON format using the MQTT protocol. The MQTT protocol was chosen for its lightweight nature and efficient message delivery, making it ideal for IoT applications. The scripts were designed to generate realistic sensor readings that could be used for testing and development purposes.
iotSimulator.teamBody: Working closely with team members, I helped define the system architecture and establish communication protocols. We designed a scalable system that could handle multiple sensor types and data streams simultaneously. The integration with Azure IoT Hub was crucial for cloud-based data storage and management.
iotSimulator.featuresBody: I contributed to the overall project by ensuring reliable data transmission between the simulator and Azure IoT Hub. Additionally, I assisted with implementing threshold-based alerts that would trigger notifications when sensor readings exceeded predefined limits. The system also included dashboard integration for real-time visualization, allowing users to monitor sensor data as it was being generated.
iotSimulator.conclusion: This project provided valuable experience in cloud computing, IoT protocols, and team collaboration. It demonstrated the importance of designing scalable systems and integrating multiple technologies to create a comprehensive solution for real-time monitoring and data management.

valorantAnalysis.title: Data Analysis
valorantAnalysis.intro1: When I was watching the recent Valorant tournament, I was wondering what the stat distribution was by agent. All of the quickly available resources that I could find had the stats distributed by player and by match, but I was curious about which agents were doing the best overall and which ones seemed to have the most impact.
valorantAnalysis.intro2BeforeLink: So I decided to find out for myself using the data provided by
valorantAnalysis.intro2AfterLink: . In order to do this, I wrote a script to look through all of the games that were played in a specific tournament and combine the data into one dataset. Since there were some games where the data was corrupted, I chose to omit those data points.
valorantAnalysis.section2023Heading: Here are the results of the data from Valorant Champions 2023:
valorantAnalysis.body1: This data is very interesting to look at because you can see who the most played agent was and compare that to the overall stats that people playing the agent had. One of the most interesting points that stood out to me was the number of assists that KAY/O had compared to Sova. Although Sova's arrow and drone show teammates the exact location of where the enemies are, KAY/O ended up with more assists, despite only showing the general area of where they are.
valorantAnalysis.section2022Heading: But then I was wondering what the stats looked like for the 2022 Valorant Champions event as well, so I decided to look at that too:
valorantAnalysis.body2: The first thing that stood out to me was the fact that chamber was picked 115 times compared to the 15 times that he was picked in the most recent Championship. It makes sense considering how much they changed the character after seeing how strong he was, but it was still interesting to see. Another datapoint that I thought was interesting was how little Reyna was picked, even though the people who played her were extremely successful with her. In both tournaments, she had the highest ACS average. But that data does need to be taken with a grain of salt because she was picked 5 times in the most recent tournament and 2 times in the earlier tournament.
valorantAnalysis.conclusion: Overall, this was a fun project, because I was able to learn how to get data from websites and I was able to actually see meta shifts from year to year in a better way than simply looking at the pickrate of agents.

spaceshipTitanic.title: Spaceship Titanic - Kaggle Tabular ML Pipeline
spaceshipTitanic.summary: Built a leakage-safe ML pipeline for the Spaceship Titanic Kaggle competition by using GroupKFold validation on passenger groups derived from PassengerId, while keeping a shared feature pipeline for train/test parity.
spaceshipTitanic.altCover: Stylized illustration of the Spaceship Titanic drifting through a colorful cosmic anomaly
spaceshipTitanic.kaggleLinkBefore: Full problem statement and dataset are on the
spaceshipTitanic.edaIntro: Before modeling I dug into how each field relates to the Transported target. A handful of clear patterns emerged that drove the entire feature engineering plan.
spaceshipTitanic.altTargetBalance: Bar chart of Transported vs Not Transported counts in the training set
spaceshipTitanic.captionTargetBalance: The target is essentially balanced — 49.6% Not Transported vs 50.4% Transported — so accuracy is a reasonable headline metric.
spaceshipTitanic.altCryoSleep: Bar chart showing transport rate for CryoSleep True vs False
spaceshipTitanic.captionCryoSleep: CryoSleep is by far the strongest single signal: passengers in CryoSleep are transported ~82% of the time vs ~33% otherwise. This motivated imputing missing CryoSleep values from total spend.
spaceshipTitanic.altSpendDistribution: Histogram of log(1 + total spend) split by Transported outcome
spaceshipTitanic.captionSpendDistribution: Transported passengers are heavily concentrated at zero spend (the spike on the left) — a direct consequence of CryoSleep — while non-transported passengers dominate the higher-spend tail.
spaceshipTitanic.altHomePlanet: Horizontal bar chart of transport rate by HomePlanet
spaceshipTitanic.captionHomePlanet: Europa passengers are transported ~66% of the time, Earth passengers only ~42%. HomePlanet is one of the few categorical fields with a strong, clean effect on the target.
spaceshipTitanic.altGroupSize: Bar chart of transport rate by passenger group size
spaceshipTitanic.captionGroupSize: Solo travelers (group size 1) are transported less often than larger groups, and the rate climbs through groups of 2–5 before flattening at 6+ — which is why passenger groups are treated as first-class entities throughout the pipeline.
spaceshipTitanic.pipelineBody1: I focused on preventing leakage by splitting data with GroupKFold around passenger groups, which prevented passengers from the same group appearing in both training and validation folds.
spaceshipTitanic.pipelineBody2: The project used a single, reproducible feature pipeline for both training and inference so transformations, encodings, and missing-value handling stayed consistent across all datasets.
spaceshipTitanic.feature1: Parsed Cabin into Deck/Num/Side, binned cabin numbers, and added a CabinMissing flag so the model can lean on cabin structure even when values are absent.
spaceshipTitanic.feature2: Built spend features (TotalExpenses, log1p per amenity, NumAmenitiesUsed, NoSpend, SpendMissingCount) and used total spend to impute missing CryoSleep values.
spaceshipTitanic.feature3: Group-aware imputation: filled HomePlanet, Destination, CabinDeck, and CabinSide using the mode within each PassengerId group, with explicit *_GroupImputed indicator flags.
spaceshipTitanic.modelsBody1: Trained and compared two strong tabular baselines — CatBoost (categoricals handled natively) and HistGradientBoosting (with integer-encoded categoricals) — under the same GroupKFold protocol for fair evaluation.
spaceshipTitanic.modelsBody2: Both models surface the same top signals: CryoSleep, total spend, and per-amenity spend dominate, which lines up with what the EDA already suggested.
spaceshipTitanic.altCatBoostImportance: CatBoost top-20 feature importance bar chart
spaceshipTitanic.captionCatBoostImportance: CatBoost feature importance — CryoSleep, Spa, VRDeck and TotalExpenses_log lead, confirming the spend-and-cryo story from the EDA.
spaceshipTitanic.altHgbPermutation: HistGradientBoosting permutation importance top-20 bar chart
spaceshipTitanic.captionHgbPermutation: HistGradientBoosting permutation importance ranks the same features at the top, providing an independent confirmation that the signal is real and not a model artifact.
spaceshipTitanic.resultsBody: Achieved a 0.804 public leaderboard score on Kaggle (rank 627 at time of submission), with stable GroupKFold cross-validation accuracy in the same range — the small CV-vs-LB gap was the main payoff of the leakage-safe split.
spaceshipTitanic.takeaway1: Group leakage is real: splitting passengers from the same booking across folds inflated CV scores and led to LB disappointment until I switched to GroupKFold.
spaceshipTitanic.takeaway2: Spend ↔ CryoSleep is the strongest signal in this dataset; deriving NoSpend, TotalExpenses_log, and imputing CryoSleep from spend improved both stability and accuracy.
spaceshipTitanic.takeaway3: Simple, robust transforms (log1p on spending, coarse age and cabin-number bins) consistently beat fancier tricks on this tabular problem.
spaceshipTitanic.reproBody: Packaged the project as a reproducible Poetry repository with a shared feature pipeline, scripted training for both models, saved artifacts and feature-importance plots, and a small report-charts script that regenerates every figure on this page from the raw CSVs.

herbSearch.title: Herb Search - Text Adventure Game
herbSearch.intro1: Herb Search is an interactive text-based adventure game built with React and TypeScript. You play as a character helping their grandma search for herbs in her house. The game features a terminal-style interface with command-based gameplay, creating an immersive retro computing experience.
herbSearch.projectFocusText: build an immersive browser-based text adventure with a strong command parser, replayability, and maintainable frontend architecture.
herbSearch.gameplayBody1: The game presents a nostalgic terminal-style interface where players interact with the world through text commands. You start by entering your name, then explore grandma's house, talk to characters, search for items, and solve puzzles. The game features a command parser that understands natural language commands like 'talk grandma', 'look around', 'go north', and more.
herbSearch.gameplayBody2: The world is procedurally generated using Perlin noise, creating a unique map layout for each playthrough. Players can explore different rooms, interact with NPCs, manage an inventory system, and track their progress through various game statistics.
herbSearch.technicalBody1: Built with React and TypeScript, the game uses a component-based architecture with custom hooks for keyboard sound effects and game state management. The terminal interface features a custom cursor that follows text input, creating an authentic command-line experience.
herbSearch.technicalBody2: Game state is persisted using localStorage, allowing players to save their progress and resume their adventure later. The command handler system processes user input and routes commands to appropriate handlers, supporting both synchronous and asynchronous operations.
herbSearch.feature2: Procedurally generated world using Perlin noise
herbSearch.feature3: Interactive NPCs with AI-powered dialogue (via backend API)
herbSearch.feature6: Terminal-style UI with custom cursor and keyboard sound effects
herbSearch.backendBody1: The game integrates with a Python FastAPI backend for AI-powered NPC conversations. When players talk to characters like grandma, the backend uses language models to generate contextual and dynamic dialogue responses, making each conversation feel unique and natural.
herbSearch.backendBody2: The backend is containerized with Docker and can be easily deployed. It handles conversation state management and provides a RESTful API for the frontend to interact with NPCs.
herbSearch.conclusion: Herb Search combines nostalgic text adventure gameplay with modern web technologies, creating an engaging and interactive experience. The project demonstrates skills in React development, game design, API integration, and creating immersive user interfaces.
